title: mobile-handshake-latency-bandwidth-profiles-annotated-scratchpad
body:
Purpose:
This scratchpad captures an early lab run measuring the impact of connection handshake and low-bandwidth profiles on end-to-end perceived latency and per-query cost for short-turn chat interactions. The goal is pragmatic: derive simple knobs (compress, early-stream, reuse) we can ship as console defaults + an experimental HTTP/3 switch for mobile clients.

Summary findings (short):
- Handshake + TLS setup adds a fixed latency floor that dominates for short responses on poor networks.
- For constrained bandwidth (<=1 Mbps) serialization size (JSON + metadata) becomes the single biggest driver of wall-clock token arrival time.
- Streaming (server-first-chunk) reduces perceived latency by ~30-60% vs waiting for full response in constrained nets, even when backend decode time is constant.
- QUIC/HTTP3 reduces tail in high-RTT scenarios by avoiding head-of-line blocking and faster connection establishment in practice.

Experimental setup (simple reproducible):
- Client emulator: tc/netem profiles on Linux VMs to simulate three network classes.
- Edge proxy: Envoy (HTTP/2) at edge node; separate run with envoy+quic (experimental).
- Backend: dedicated Redwood Dedicated cluster (a4x16-like profile) running a 13B decoder model. Backend decode times measured independently: p50 120ms, p95 210ms for a 64 token output on this machine.
- Requests: 3 turn types: 
  1) Short prompt (user->system): 32 tokens prompt, expected 8-16 token reply (e.g., quick confirmation).
  2) Medium: 128 token prompt, 64 token reply (document summary).
  3) Long: 512 token prompt, 256 token reply (long completion).
- Serialization: default JSON payload with authorization header, request/response metadata. Baseline payload sizes measured.

Network profiles used (apparent RTT and bandwidth):
- Good mobile: RTT 40ms, BW 20-70 Mbps (we used 40 Mbps).
- Constrained mobile: RTT 120ms, BW 1 Mbps.
- Satellite: RTT 600ms, BW 100 kbps.

Measured components (how we break down latency):
- C_conn: Connection/TLS handshake (including TCP + TLS 1.3 RT)
- C_request_tx: Client upload time (bytes / upstream_bw + RTT/2 assumptions)
- C_edge_proc: Edge proxy processing (small, ~5-12ms)
- C_backend_queuing+decode: Backend wait + model decode (measured separately)
- C_stream_first_byte: Time to first response byte arriving to client (includes server writing first chunk)
- C_full: Time until last response byte received

Baseline payload sizes (approx):
- Short request (headers+json): 1.2 KB
- Short response (uncompressed): 1.8 KB per 16 tokens (JSON-wrapped chunks)
- Overhead: TLS handshake packet bytes ~1.2 KB * initial flows but not dominant in bytes, dominant in RTTs.

Selected run results (annotated):
ASCII chart: perceived time to first token (ms) and time-to-complete (ms) for short-turn (32->16)

Network       | C_conn | C_request_tx | C_edge | backend_p50 | first_token | full_complete
--------------|--------|--------------|--------|-------------|-------------|--------------
Good (40ms)   | 80 ms  | 5 ms         | 8 ms   | 120 ms      | 210 ms      | 260 ms
Constrained   | 240 ms | 1000 ms      | 10 ms  | 120 ms      | 1370 ms     | 1600 ms
Satellite     | 1200 ms| 2000 ms      | 18 ms  | 120 ms      | 3338 ms     | 3600 ms

Notes on values: C_conn approximated as 2 RTTs for TLS1.3 full handshake in our env (client+server cert steps, connection warmup). C_request_tx = payload / available upstream bw + RTT/2 overlapped. Backend_p50 is fixed for model; first_token reflects earliest server pushed chunk arrival to client. Full_complete includes mobile reassembly and final byte arrival.

Key derived metrics:
- Fraction of end-to-end latency due to network (short-turn): Good ~35%, Constrained ~85%, Satellite ~95% (network dominates at low BW/high RTT).
- Cost impact (back-of-envelope): additional perceived waiting time costs product engagement but also raises token billing window for streaming-based metering in some plans. For compute cost, backend runtime unchanged; however for Reserved capacity planning, high bandwidth-induced serialization delays lengthen slot occupancy and reduce throughput-per-GPU in practice (we observed effective throughput drop ~12% in constrained runs due to longer outstanding sessions).

Comparing strategies (short notes):
1) Early streaming (first-chunk-size tuned to 16–32 bytes of model text + minimal JSON):
   - Reduces perceived TTFB by 30–60% across constrained profiles. Overhead: increases number of small packets; careful use of gzip helps.
2) Compression on wire (gzip for small JSON fields):
   - For 1 KB->300 bytes common, savings large in <=1 Mbps. Decompression cheap on client.
3) HTTP/3 (QUIC):
   - Reduces C_conn significantly (0-1 RTT faster in our env) and avoids head-of-line blocking in satellite runs. Observed 18–40% reduction in p95 of first token for high-RTT.
4) Connection reuse / keepalive:
   - Massive wins for conversational clients: avoid repeated C_conn cost per turn. Recommend sticky websockets or long-lived HTTP/2 connections from SDK.

Small ASCII sensitivity table: TTFB delta (streaming vs no-streaming) at constrained BW

Scenario                | no-stream(ms) | streaming(ms) | delta(ms)
------------------------|---------------|---------------|----------
short-turn (32->16)     | 1600          | 920           | -680
medium (128->64)        | 2600          | 1900          | -700
long (512->256)         | 7200          | 6000          | -1200

Interpretation: streaming benefit is largest in absolute ms for long outputs but largest fraction for short-turns because backend time is smaller.

Operational implications (recommendations):
- SDK defaults: enable persistent HTTP/2 connections + gzip payload compression for mobile SDKs.
- Console UX: surface a toggle and recommendation to enable HTTP/3 for edge deployments (note: experimental in some clouds).
- Edge config: allow small initial chunk strategy and auto-adapt chunk size to measured client RTT/BW (heuristic: first chunk targets < 200ms transmit at measured upstream BW).
- Billing note: document streaming vs full response token accounting differences in billing docs so customers know perceived vs billable windows.

Open questions / next steps (lab TODOs):
- Repeat with real phones (iOS/Android) and carrier networks; emulator profiles are approximations.
- Measure interaction with TLS 0-RTT (if we enable session resumption) on client cold start patterns.
- Validate memory / slot occupancy impact on Dedicated pools when sessions are long-running due to network slowness; we saw a 10–15% effective throughput drop in the constrained runs but need larger sample.
- Try binary payload path (protobuf) and CBOR vs JSON for additional savings.

Appendix: quick commands used
- tc/netem example: sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 120ms loss 0% rate 1mbit
- curl streaming test: curl -v --http2 -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' --data-binary @short.json https://edge.redwood/api/v1/generate

References / links
- JIRA INF-1423 (mobile handshake benchmarks)
- GH runtime#2894 (edge QUIC experiment)

Contact: Priya Desai (eng-observability) — ping in #observability for live runs and dataset attachments.
